name: non arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy

clinicalPearls: Most common acute optic neuropathy in patients over 50; typically painless, sudden, monocular loss often noticed on waking.
An inferior altitudinal visual field defect is the classic pattern, though any nerve-fibre-bundle defect may occur.
The structural predisposition is a small, crowded optic disc with a small or absent physiological cup, the so-called disc at risk, best appreciated in the fellow eye.
Vasculopathic risk factors predominate: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea and nocturnal hypotension.
At onset the disc shows segmental or diffuse hyperaemic oedema with peripapillary splinter haemorrhages, later resolving to sectoral pallor.
A relative afferent pupillary defect is present unless there is bilateral or previous fellow-eye involvement.
There is no proven effective treatment; the essential immediate step is to exclude an arteritic (giant cell arteritis) cause.
Fellow-eye involvement occurs in a meaningful minority over subsequent years, so vascular risk-factor modification is advised.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder results from transient hypoperfusion or non-perfusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries supplying the laminar and prelaminar anterior optic nerve head. In a structurally crowded disc with little room for swelling, the initial ischaemic insult produces axonal oedema that raises tissue pressure within the confined scleral canal, creating a compartment-like effect that compresses capillaries and propagates further ischaemia. The process is neither embolic nor inflammatory in most cases, distinguishing it from arteritic and retinal arterial occlusive disease.
additionalDifferentials: Arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy from giant cell arteritis
Central retinal vein occlusion with disc oedema
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein and platelet count to exclude giant cell arteritis
Blood pressure assessment including consideration of nocturnal hypotension
Fasting glucose or glycated haemoglobin and a fasting lipid profile
Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Automated perimetry to document the field defect
Screening for obstructive sleep apnoea where clinically suggested
Neuroimaging with magnetic resonance imaging if the presentation is atypical
redFlags: Symptoms of giant cell arteritis such as jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache or polymyalgia rheumatica
Pain on eye movement suggesting optic neuritis rather than ischaemia
Progressive rather than static visual loss suggesting a compressive or infiltrative cause
Simultaneous bilateral involvement warranting urgent systemic evaluation
reference.prognosis: Visual acuity commonly stabilises after the acute event and a proportion of patients show modest spontaneous improvement. Recurrence in the same eye is uncommon, but fellow-eye involvement occurs in roughly one in six to one in five patients over several years.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude giant cell arteritis and thereby missing a treatable, sight-threatening arteritic cause
Misattributing the presentation to optic neuritis in an older vasculopathic patient
Not screening for obstructive sleep apnoea and modifiable vascular risk factors
Assuming corticosteroids provide benefit, for which evidence is lacking
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course, Neuro-Ophthalmology
management: Aggressively modify vasculopathic risk factors — control hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia with antihypertensives, glucose-lowering therapy and a statin
Avoid nocturnal hypotension by reviewing antihypertensive timing and cautioning against evening dosing, and advise avoidance of phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors
Urgently exclude giant cell arteritis with inflammatory markers before attributing the event to the non-arteritic form, given the sight-threatening fellow-eye risk of untreated arteritis
Investigate for and treat obstructive sleep apnoea with continuous positive airway pressure where identified
Provide low-vision rehabilitation and visual aids for the residual altitudinal field defect
Counsel on the substantial risk of fellow-eye involvement, monitor the second eye, and advise prompt review of any new visual symptoms
Refer to neuro-ophthalmology for confirmation, OCT and perimetry monitoring, and exclusion of non-arteritic mimics
